course.title: Community Manager Certification
course.subtitle: The Vegans Explore Community Manager handbook, as a course
course.summary: Everything you need to lead a Vegans Explore community: the role, the agreement, businesses and partners, engaging your community, events and Community Nights, structure, standards and conduct. Pass every module at 80% or above to be certified.

pages.title: Visibility is the job
pages.content:
Without someone taking responsibility for visibility, the work happening in a community effectively disappears, even when it is real and thriving. If there is no platform or presence showing that work, people have no reason to believe there is anything active to support. Engagement dies quietly, not because the community failed, but because nobody could see it.

Your job, at its core: make people aware that others in your city are working toward this cause and need their support. Be the constant reminder that shows up, whatever is happening in someone's life: an event, a post, a message that reminds them there is something real they can plug back into.

Food is the way in

Great plant-based food gets people through the door. Once they are in, they discover the real reason behind the Vegan message: the animals. That is the path Vegans Explore builds, and you are the one holding the door open in your city.

pages.title: Your first days
pages.content:
Day one: get full awareness of every opportunity currently active in your city. Enterprise and sponsor-level opportunities, once those relationships are locked in, arrive as project briefs pushed to your dashboard, with specific detail on what that opportunity requires of you.

Your first week

  • Complete this certification.
  • Walk through vegansexplore.com/partners start to finish, the way a business would.
  • Set a call with Sean to plan your city's first night.
  • Start your list of businesses, organizations and volunteers.

You lead locally. The team backs you with the technology, the platform, the guidance and more than ten years of best practices, and takes on the larger partnerships.

pages.title: Volunteering, with a stipend
pages.content:
This is not a part-time job. It is volunteering, with a stipend because you go a little above and beyond what a volunteer does.

  • Three-month trial. So we can both see if it is a fit.
  • $250 a month stipend. It covers your regular role, about 3 hours a week and rarely more than 5: the weekly check-in, messages, attending your city's events, and capturing photos, contacts and leads. It starts once your Founding Membership goes through and is paid each month on the date you registered.
  • Additional stipends. Managing an event or being assigned to a campaign comes with its own additional stipend, and what you earn grows as your region grows. When a bigger campaign or project comes in, enterprise deals or sponsors, there is always a line item in that budget for the Community Manager.

The expectation: keep your community thriving and growing, and help it pay for itself by signing up members and partner businesses.

Built for the long haul

As membership revenue in your city grows, the role grows with it, toward a full salary once it justifies a full-time position. There is one Community Manager per region, and every city also has someone working alongside you and learning from you, training to become a Community Coordinator, so no city ever has to start from zero.

pages.title: The directory and the first relationship
pages.content:
There is, or will be, a directory of every Vegan business in your area: The LESARUSS Directory. Your job is to make sure those businesses are in it and to reach out so they claim their listing. That outreach is the beginning of the relationship. Templates and resources are provided; you are there to be a real human point of contact.

Once a business claims its listing, it gets an official email address used through its own dashboard, and communications happen there. Some of the process is automated. Anything that specifically needs you shows up in your queue as a notification: open it and follow the instructions inside.

Three roles in the process: the agent (automation), the business (the customer) and you (the human touchpoint).

Vegans Explore itself stays a top-of-funnel, nonprofit-facing layer: awareness, coordination and front-end visibility. When a business genuinely wants a commercial relationship, it moves to The LESARUSS Directory and LESARUSS AI layer, where paid services are pitched and sold. What closes there counts toward your performance pay.

pages.title: How partners come in
pages.content:
Say the line, then share the link. The line: we put your food in front of people who have not tried plant-based yet, at nights they actually want to go to. The link: vegansexplore.com/partners.

  1. They tap Become a member and make a one-time $11 contribution.
  2. They answer a few quick questions and see their options, with pricing.
  3. They lock in a Community Night table or goodie bags, or book a call with Sean for larger partnerships.
  4. You get an email with what they chose, and you make sure they get it.

Local questions and purchases from your city come to your inbox with Sean copied. Answer them directly. You are their person.

Every partner gets a report within 7 days of each event. That is how we keep our word.

pages.title: Finding your people
pages.content:
Look for people already doing the work before you find them: hosting workshops, volunteering at events, posting on social media, showing up consistently. Festivals are the single best place to find them in person, which is why Vegans Explore needs to be at festivals networking and connecting, not just tabling. The other reliable source is your own events: the people who keep showing up when you host are already self-selecting.

A lot of the time they find you first: at a festival table, in your event crowd, in your comments. The job is recognizing them in the moment and moving fast. Get them signed up and into the ecosystem immediately. Do not let that moment pass.

pages.title: Leading online and keeping people close
pages.content:
You lead your city's conversations as well as the room. Our community conversations belong on our platform, not in WhatsApp groups, and as they come online you lead your city's. Use the platform to bring your city together, online and in person, and enroll people as members and volunteers, not just attendees. Members power our points system, the app on the way and what comes next.

Once people are in, the system carries the ongoing relationship, not your memory. Automation handles the routine touchpoints. When a real human moment is needed, it surfaces in your queue. Your job is to be ready to act on what shows up in front of you.

Churn is normal, consistency is the job

People come and go. Do not get locked into any one person staying forever. What has to stay constant is you. Your job is to help people stay as long as they realistically can.

Because Vegans Explore is multi-city, someone leaving your city is not a pure loss: they can join another Vegans Explore community, and you gain people moving in from other cities.

questions.question: Where is the single best place to find future Explorers in person?
When someone who is already doing the work shows up in front of you, what should you do?
options: Recognize them and get them signed up into the ecosystem right away

questions.question: Who carries the ongoing relationship once someone is in?
options: The system, with human moments surfacing in your queue

questions.question: How should you think about people leaving your community?
options: It is a failure to be avoided at all costs

It means the city should close

pages.title: Someone from Vegans Explore is in the room
pages.content:
The website houses every event happening in your city, so the standing expectation is simple: you are at each of those events, or you have delegated it to a volunteer or Vegan Explorer on your team who is.

At the event: make sure everybody there knows about Vegans Explore, ideally converting them into members, run some fun on-site activation, and connect people to the digital side of the platform while they are physically present. If you do not already have a relationship with the event owner, building one is part of the job.

After the event: capture content, photos and video, enough for a short recap or article, either yourself or through people on your team. That content goes into the regular content stream so people who missed it know these things are happening, and so the event owner sees Vegans Explore showed up and delivered.

pages.title: Coordinating our own events
pages.content:
When it is a Vegans Explore event rather than someone else's, you are the coordinator: pulling the team together, sourcing opportunities and managing the logistics the event requires.

You are the direct liaison with headquarters, receiving directives from Sean or senior leadership. When Sean or a senior leader is coming in person, your job is making sure everything is set up, connected and ready to receive them.

This applies across festivals, outdoor events and indoor events. Local event storage gets funded once your city lands a sponsorship or vendor relationship. A per-event-type SOP lays out what each event type entails and what each team member on site is responsible for.

pages.title: A party, not a presentation
pages.content:
A Community Night is a party, not a presentation. The format flexes with the partner and the place (a party, an outdoor night) and moves around the region so every night feels fresh.

What the night includes

  • Food, sampling and vendor tables
  • Goodie bags
  • Something fun for the room, like a costume contest or a DJ
  • Check-in is the membership signup
  • A sponsor stamp card that drives table traffic into a prize drawing
  • One five-minute moment from the DJ booth that tells the room what we are building

You run the back table: the place where people check in, become members and connect to what comes next.

pages.title: Rules that protect the night
pages.content:
• Food: sampling only, unless a vendor holds the right temporary food event permit.
  • Paid influencer posts: always carry clear #ad disclosure.
  • Money language: partnerships are marketing partnerships. No tax-deductible language anywhere.
  • Numbers: never quote a reach or audience number without a cited source.
  • Stadium nights: follow the venue's rules. For the Dolphins game night: no sales on the grounds, and no bags into the stadium, which is why goodie bags are picked up at a Community Night beforehand.
  • After every event: each partner gets a report within 7 days.

pages.title: The weekly hot lab and your authority
pages.content:
The main structural touchpoint is a weekly check-in with all Community Managers at once, not one-on-ones. It works as a hot lab: each city reports what is working and what is not, questions get asked in front of the group, and HQ shares updates on big projects and opportunities. Longer term, a Community Coordinator, hired from within the Community Manager ranks, runs the weekly meeting, and Sean's time goes to bigger state-of-the-nation conversations.

Be the first to know

You are our eyes and ears in your city. When a Vegan restaurant opens, closes or starts adding animal products, or the community is talking about a controversy, we should hear it from you first. Come to the huddle ready to share what is happening, what you are up against and what you want to try. We celebrate the cities that grow, and we rally around the ones that need support.

Day to day, your authority is deliberately prescribed: what is on your plate is spelled out. It is not an open mandate to decide direction.

New ideas are welcome, and the weekly meeting is where they surface. On purpose, they are not decided or built in a silo by one city. They go to the whole group so the team can react, collaborate and build the idea together, because anything you build is part of the shared Vegans Explore ecosystem.

pages.title: How we know it is working
pages.content:
Doing well is responsive and proactive, and it shows up as measurable signals, not a gut feeling.

  • Reports are due at set times and roll up into a dashboard HQ sees across every city.
  • Business health: the platform scores the health of the Vegan businesses connected to your community. Keep that score inside the expected range.
  • Coverage: show up to events, or make sure there is always coverage when you cannot be there.
  • Community feedback: members can flag issues directly, and it feeds the same picture.
  • Growth: month-over-month growth in your community's size is tracked as a hard number.

Your monthly scorecard: events attended, contacts logged, warm introductions, and three qualified sponsor conversations a month.

Think of it like being a principal at a school: real latitude to shape culture and gather your community, alongside following the rules HQ sets.

questions.question: How is performance measured?
options: By measurable signals such as reports, business health, coverage, feedback and growth

questions.question: How many qualified sponsor conversations a month are on the scorecard?
If you cannot be at an event yourself, what is expected?
options: Make sure there is coverage from your team

questions.question: What does the business health score reflect?
options: How well you are managing the Vegan businesses connected to your community

pages.title: How we show up
pages.content:
Tardiness

Zero tolerance. Showing up even one minute late is unacceptable, and it counts against you, potentially leading to removal after a review.

Reviews are seasonal

Every LESARUSS brand runs in seasons, not calendar quarters, tied to the 111 Day Theory. Community Managers are reviewed at season boundaries. Because the date is fixed and known in advance, you will know where you stand well before the season ends. If direction is changing, that conversation starts before the cutoff, never as a surprise.

Professional boundaries when money is involved

Build real, authentic relationships with your community. At the same time, keep a deliberate separation: you will handle money and sometimes deliver news that lets someone down, like a deal falling through or a missed payment. Build the relationship, and be able to switch to stern and professional the moment it is a business matter.

questions.question: What is the standard on lateness?
options: Zero tolerance: even one minute late counts against you

questions.question: When are Community Managers reviewed?
options: At season boundaries, tied to the 111 Day Theory
Only when there is a problem

questions.question: Why will a review never be a surprise?
options: The date is fixed and known in advance, and any change in direction is discussed before the cutoff

questions.question: How should you handle a partner's missed payment?
options: Ignore it to keep the friendship
Switch to stern and professional; it is a business matter
